lessons.title: Word order as the speaker's tool: what final position does, and where не goes
lessons.explanation: Russian word order is free in the sense that grammar does not fix it, and unfree in the sense that information structure does. Cornell's Beginning Russian Grammar states the rule in one line: 'The general rule for Russian word order is to put new information at the end of the sentence.' Ask Кто представил Сашу? (kto preed-STA-veet SA-shoo), 'who introduced Sasha?', and the answer is Сашу представила Маша (SA-shoo preed-STA-vee-la MA-sha), with the name in final position. The neutral order Маша представила Сашу is equally grammatical; it answers a different question, and a learner who uses it to answer the question about the introducer sounds as if the important word were Сашу. Written Russian leans on this more heavily than speech because it has no intonation to fall back on: Cornell notes that a speaker can accent the subject in initial position, but that in written Russian 'that auditory option is not available', so the Object plus Verb plus Subject order does the work. Three positions carry the load. Final position carries the new or contrastive element. Initial position carries the topic, the thing already under discussion, and it also marks emphasis when the element is an adverb: alphaDictionary observes that 'initial position is reserved for emphasized adverbs', so Часто он ходит в библиотеку (CHAS-ta on KHO-deet v beeb-lee-a-TYE-koo), 'often he goes to the library', foregrounds the frequency. Position relative to the noun decides what an adjective is doing: red in front is attributive, red behind is a predicate or an emphatic aside, so красный дом (KRAS-ny DOM) is 'the red house' while дом красный (DOM KRAS-ny) is 'the house is red'. Negation has its own positional logic, and this is where learners do the most damage. не negates the constituent that follows it, not the whole sentence by default. Мария не купила билет (ma-REE-ya ne koo-PEE-la bee-LYET) denies the purchase. Мария купила не билет, а абонемент (ma-REE-ya koo-PEE-la ne bee-LYET, a a-ba-nee-MENT) denies the object and asserts another one. Не Мария купила билет, а Сергей (ne ma-REE-ya koo-PEE-la bee-LYET, a seer-GYEY) denies the agent. Those three sentences share every word and differ only in where не stands, which is why lesson 103 treats scope as a topic in its own right.
lessons.example: Read the four orders aloud, then say which question each one answers. 1. Мария купила билеты. (ma-REE-ya koo-PEE-la bee-LYE-ty.) 'Maria bought the tickets.' Neutral, and the answer to 'what happened?'. 2. Билеты купила Мария. (bee-LYE-ty koo-PEE-la ma-REE-ya.) 'Maria was the one who bought the tickets.' Final position carries the answer to 'who bought the tickets?'. 3. Билеты Мария купила. (bee-LYE-ty ma-REE-ya koo-PEE-la.) 'The tickets, Maria did buy.' The verb is final and therefore contrastive, and the sentence implies a 'but' to follow: she bought them but did not pay for them. 4. Мария купила не билеты, а абонементы. (ma-REE-ya koo-PEE-la ne bee-LYE-ty, a a-ba-nee-MEN-ty.) 'Maria bought not tickets but season passes.' Now a short written paragraph in the register of a report, where the same machinery does the work without a voice to help it. В понедельник отдел согласовал смету. Смету согласовал директор, а не начальник отдела. Директор согласовал смету, но не график. (f pa-nee-DYEL-neek at-DYEL sag-la-SO-val SMYE-too. SMYE-too sag-la-SO-val dee-RYEK-tar, a ne na-CHAL-neek at-DYEL-la. dee-RYEK-tar sag-la-SO-val SMYE-too, no ne GRA-feek.) 'On Monday the department approved the estimate. It was the director, not the head of department, who approved the estimate. The director approved the estimate but not the schedule.' Watch what the three sentences do in sequence. The first is neutral and sets the topic: the department, the estimate, Monday. The second repeats смету in initial position precisely so that it stays topic, and then puts the true actor last, which reverses the first sentence without contradicting it. The third keeps the actor first because the actor is now the topic, and puts the contrast at the end after но не. Nothing in the paragraph needs a new ending: the accusative смету and the nominative директор are what allow each element to move, and the movement is what makes the paragraph readable. A learner who writes all three sentences in subject-first order produces a text that is grammatical on every line and unreadable as a whole, because every line claims to be answering the same question.
lessons.question: A colleague asks «Кто согласовал смету?» (kto sag-la-SO-val SMYE-too) and you answer «Директор согласовал смету». What is wrong with the answer, and what should it be?
lessons.answer: The new information, директор, is not in final position, so the reply reads as a statement about the estimate rather than as an answer to who approved it; the natural reply is «Смету согласовал директор».
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because Russian word order is free and every order answers the question equally well.
lessons.correction: The order is free in the sense that no ending changes, and not free in the sense that the answer depends on it. The question asks for an actor, and Russian puts the new element last, so the actor belongs at the end: Смету согласовал директор. The distracter confuses grammatical freedom with communicative indifference, which is the single most common misconception about this topic. A Spanish or Italian speaker has an advantage here, because those languages also move the subject to the end for focus, but English word order makes the transfer hard: 'The director approved the estimate' is the only unmarked order in English, and translating it word for word produces exactly the wrong answer.

depth.definitions: Information structure is the division of a sentence into what the hearer already knows (тема, TYE-ma, 'theme, topic') and what is being asserted about it (рема, RYE-ma, 'rheme, comment'). Neutral order means the order used when nothing is being contrasted. Contrastive position means the position that carries the correction of an expectation, and in Russian that is normally the final position, with the initial position used for a contrastive adverb. Scope of negation is the part of the sentence that не actually denies: in Мария не купила билет it is the purchase, in Мария купила не билет it is the object, in Не Мария купила билет it is the agent. Attributive position means the adjective stands before its noun and names a property; predicate position means it stands after the noun and asserts the property. Prerequisites: the case system of lessons 51 to 54 supplies the markings that make movement possible, and lesson 91 used the same final-position principle to read a news report rather than to build one.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism is a trade that Russian makes and English does not. Because nouns carry case, a noun's job in the sentence is visible from its ending, so its position is free to carry discourse information instead. English has lost most of its case endings, so position has to do the grammatical job, and a sentence like 'The director approved the estimate' cannot be reordered without changing which noun is the subject. Russian can reorder because смету is accusative and cannot be mistaken for the subject, and because директор is nominative and cannot be mistaken for the object. This is why word order in Russian is a consequence of the case system rather than a decorative option: a learner who has not automated the endings cannot use the order safely, because moving a noun without knowing its case produces a different sentence rather than a differently organised one. The second mechanism is the placement of не. Russian does not move не to the end of the sentence and does not negate the verb by default; не stands immediately before the constituent it denies, and everything after не inherits the denial until the next contrast. This is why «не билет, а абонемент» works as a single piece: the не marks the first element and а marks the correction.
depth.secondExample: Here is the same machinery in a service exchange, where the stakes are immediate. «Извините, этот документ подписал директор?» (eez-vee-NEE-tye, EH-tat da-koo-MENT POD-pee-sal dee-RYEK-tar?) 'Excuse me, was it the director who signed this document?' «Документ подписал заместитель директора, а директор его только видел.» (da-koo-MENT POD-pee-sal za-MYES-tee-tyel dee-RYEK-ta-ra, a dee-RYEK-tar ee-VO TOL-ka VEE-deel.) 'The deputy director signed the document; the director only saw it.' Three things are worth extracting. First, the question and the answer share an order, документ first, because both speakers hold the document as the topic; the answer differs only in the final element, which is what a correction looks like. Second, the correction is done with а plus the negated alternative implied, not with a blunt нет: the clerk never says 'no', which is the register point that lesson 87 made about disagreement. Third, only видел is left unqualified at the end of the second clause, and that final position is what carries the sting: the director saw it, and that is all he did. A learner who answers «Нет, документ подписал заместитель» is not wrong, but the flat нет followed by the same order gives the correction without the topic chain, and the hearer has to reconstruct what the two sentences have in common.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first is keeping English subject-first order for every sentence and relying on a rising tone to mark the question, which works in speech and collapses in writing. Diagnostic: read your paragraph and ask of each sentence what question it answers; if every sentence answers 'what happened?', the paragraph has no information structure. The second is placing не at the end or before the verb when the denial is aimed at a noun, producing «Мария купила билет не» or «Мария не купила билет, а абонемент» where the second clause then contradicts the first. Diagnostic: underline the word after не; if that is not the word you mean to deny, move не. The third is specific to speakers of Spanish and Italian, who are used to postnominal adjectives and produce «билеты новые» intending 'new tickets'. In Russian that order reads as a predicate, 'the tickets are new', so the transfer changes a description into a claim. Diagnostic: if the adjective is doing descriptive work, put it in front; if it is doing assertive work, leave it behind and be ready for the sentence to sound like an answer rather than a label.
depth.application: Take one neutral sentence of your own with a subject, a verb and an object, for example «Коллега отправил отчёт» (ka-LEE-ga at-PRA-veet at-CHOT), 'a colleague sent the report'. Write it four times: neutral, actor final, object initial with the verb final, and with не before each of the three content words in turn. Beside each version write the question it answers, in Russian if you can, and mark which word carries the new information. Then do the same with one sentence from a Russian news item you have already read in lesson 91, and check whether the order in the original matches the question the paragraph is answering. Finally, read the four versions aloud and notice which one requires a pitch accent to be understood: that is the version you should avoid in writing. The whole task takes about twenty minutes and produces a four-line table that you can reuse whenever a paragraph feels flat.
depth.summary: Word order in Russian is grammatical freedom plus communicative obligation. The endings decide who does what, so position is free to decide what is new, and the new element goes last. The initial position holds the topic and, for adverbs, the emphasis; the position before or after the noun decides whether an adjective describes or asserts; не stands before the constituent it denies and carries its denial to the end of that constituent. Cornell's rule, new information last, is the one sentence to remember, and the three test sentences in this lesson are the proof that it is a rule and not a preference. What you cannot do is move words without knowing their cases, because the freedom is bought with the endings.

visual.title: Four-slot sentence map with three не insertion points
visual.description: A labeled text diagram: one clause written in four positions, with brackets under each position naming its discourse job, and a second row showing the same clause with не inserted before the object, the verb and the subject. Rendered as text steps, not as an image.
steps: Step 1, draw the slots. Write four boxes labeled 1 to 4 and put the neutral sentence «Мария купила билет» into them, one word per box. Under box 1 write 'тема, known', under box 4 write 'рема, new'. This is the baseline against which every later order is measured.

Step 2, move the actor to the end. Rewrite the sentence as «Билет купила Мария» and write above box 4 the question it answers, «Кто купил билет?». Note that no ending changed, which is the evidence that the endings, not the positions, carry the grammar.

Step 3, mark the three не sites. Under the baseline sentence write three lines, each with не inserted in a different slot: before the subject, before the verb, before the object. Beside each line write what it denies and what it implies instead. This row is the scope table that lesson 103 expands.

Step 4, label the adjective pair. Add two short lines, «красный дом» and «дом красный», and mark the first as attributive and the second as predicate. This is the one place where a change of order changes the grammatical job rather than only the emphasis.

Step 5, test against a real paragraph. Take the three-sentence report from the example and write the question each sentence answers in the margin. If any two sentences answer the same question, you have found the line that needs reordering.

lessons.title: Particles that carry the speaker's stance: же, ведь, -то, ли, разве, неужели
lessons.explanation: A particle (частица, chas-TEE-tsa) is an uninflected word that adds the speaker's attitude to a statement that is already grammatically complete. Remove it and the sentence still stands; keep it and the sentence says what the speaker thinks about what it says. Russian grammar sorts particles into classes, and the classes are worth knowing because they predict behaviour. The Russian Wikipedia article on частицы lists формообразующие частицы (бы, пусть, давай), which build moods and imperatives; отрицательные частицы (не, ни); and модальные частицы, which divide into вопросительные (ли, разве, неужели), указательные (вот, вон), уточняющие (именно, как раз), выделительные (только, лишь), восклицательные (что за, как) and усилительные (даже, ни, же, ведь, уж, всё-таки). This lesson works through the four that a learner meets on the first page of any real message: же, ведь, -то and ли. же and ведь are усилительные, intensifying: they point at something already shared and treat it as grounds for the current statement. Ты же обещал (ty zhe a-bee-SHCHAL), 'you did promise', is a reproach because the promise is treated as common ground. Ведь я предупреждал (vyet ya pree-doop-reezh-DAL), 'after all, I did warn you', is the same move with a defensive colour. -то is a topicaliser that attaches to one word with a hyphen and isolates it: Я-то помню (YA-ta POM-nyu), 'I remember, whatever he does'. ли is the interrogative particle and behaves like a clitic: it stands after the word it questions, never first, and it turns a statement into a question of fact, Знаешь ли ты (ZNA-yesh lee ty), 'do you know?'. Position is grammar for two of the four. ru.wikipedia's spelling section is blunt about the mechanics: бы, же and ли are written separately, while -то, -ка, -де and -с are written with a hyphen, which is why ты же and я-то look inconsistent until you know that they belong to different spelling rules. Register matters as much as meaning. Particles cluster in speech and in messages; formal written Russian uses them sparingly, and a particle in a report reads as a spoken aside. Lesson 82 made the written and spoken registers two grammars; particles are one of the clearest places where the difference shows, because a particle cannot be replaced by a synonym, only by a different sentence.
lessons.example: A short exchange, then the same exchange stripped of particles. «Ты же обещал позвонить.» (ty zhe a-bee-SHCHAL pa-zva-NEET.) 'You did promise to call.' «Я-то помню. А он, видимо, забыл.» (YA-ta POM-nyu. a on, VEE-dee-ma, za-BYL.) 'I remember. He, apparently, forgot.' «Разве он не звонил?» (RAZ-vee on ne zva-NEEL?) 'Didn't he call, then?' «Неужели ты думаешь, что я шучу?» (nee-oozh-EL-ee ty DOO-ma-esh, shto ya shoo-CHOO?) 'Do you really think I am joking?' «Он даже не извинился.» (on DA-zhe ne eez-vee-NEEL-sya.) 'He did not even apologise.' Now the same content as a written note, with every particle removed: Я помню. Он не звонил. Ты думаешь, что я шучу? Он не извинился. (ya POM-nyu. on ne zva-NEEL. ty DOO-ma-esh, shto ya shoo-CHOO? on ne eez-vee-NEEL-sya.) 'I remember. He did not call. You think I am joking. He did not apologise.' Every sentence is still correct and every sentence has lost its stance. The first version accuses, doubts, insists and reproaches; the second reports. That is the whole function of the class, and it is why a learner who omits particles sounds cold and a learner who sprinkles them into a report sounds unserious. Note also what the particles do to the shape of the sentence. же and ведь sit immediately after the word they lean on, so ты же keeps ты in focus. -то attaches with a hyphen and isolates its host, so я-то sets up a contrast with someone else. ли forces the word order to change, because it cannot stand first: the statement «Ты знаешь» becomes «Знаешь ли ты», with the verb first and the particle second. разве and неужели open the clause and colour the whole question, разве as mild surprise and неужели as genuine disbelief. даже precedes the element it escalates, and in «даже не извинился» it escalates the absence, not the apology.
lessons.question: Your colleague promised to send a file and did not. You write «Ты обещал отправить файл». A Russian colleague rewrites it as «Ты же обещал отправить файл». What did the particle add, and why does the position matter?
lessons.answer: же marks the promise as shared ground, so the sentence becomes a reproach rather than a report; it stands immediately after ты because that is the word being held to the promise, and it is written separately.
lessons.distractor: же means 'also', so the sentence now says that someone else promised as well, and it could equally stand at the end of the sentence.
lessons.correction: же is not 'also' and it is not 'same'. The word for 'also' is тоже or также, and neither would fit here. же is an усилительная частица that treats the statement as something the hearer already knows or has already agreed to, which is exactly the tone of a reproach: you and I both know you promised. Position is part of the meaning: after ты, the particle presses on the person; after отправить, it would press on the action. It is written separately, never with a hyphen, unlike -то. The distracter is the error of Translating the nearest English word and then treating the particle as a movable adverb, and it produces a sentence that is either wrong or meaningless in context.

depth.definitions: A particle is an uninflected word that expresses the speaker's stance toward the content of a sentence or toward its addressee, without changing the sentence's proposition. The classes named in this lesson are усилительные (intensifying: же, ведь, даже, уж, всё-таки), указательные (pointing: вот, вон), уточняющие (specifying: именно, как раз), выделительные (restricting: только, лишь) and вопросительные (questioning: ли, разве, неужели). A clitic is a word that has no stress of its own and leans on a neighbouring word; ли is a clitic and that is why it stands second in its clause. A topicaliser is a particle that marks one element as the current topic and implicitly contrasts it with something else; -то does this. Формообразующие частицы (бы, пусть, давай) are a different job altogether, because they build grammatical forms rather than comment on them, and lesson 104 treats бы in that role. Prerequisites: the reported-speech particles мол and дескать from lesson 76, the hedging vocabulary of lesson 77, and the register split of lesson 82.
depth.mechanism: Why does Russian need a whole word class for stance? Because its syntax is already fully occupied: case endings mark the roles, aspect marks the boundedness, and word order marks the information structure, so there is no slot left for 'how I feel about this'. Particles fill that slot. The mechanism is association rather than predication: a particle does not assert anything, it points at an assumption. же points at an assumption the speaker believes is shared, and the sentence then reads as a consequence of that assumption, which is why it can sound either like solidarity or like an accusation depending on the content. ведь points at an assumption the speaker is invoking as a justification, which is why it often appears in explanations and defences. -то points at an element as already identified and sets it against an alternative, which is why it produces the 'as for X' reading. ли points at the clause as an open question, and because it is unstressed it must lean on the word before it, which forces the word order. Once you see the class as pointing rather than saying, the translations stop being mysterious: each particle names a different kind of shared or open assumption, and English has to spell that out with whole phrases like 'after all', 'as for me', 'do you really'.
depth.secondExample: Here is the same class doing work in a negotiation, where the particles decide who has to justify what. «Ведь мы договаривались о сроках.» (vyet my da-ga-VA-ree-va-lees a SRO-kakh.) 'After all, we did agree on the deadlines.' «Договаривались-то мы, но вы же сами просили перенести.» (da-ga-VA-ree-va-lees-ta my, no vy zhe SA-mee pra-SEE-lee pee-ree-nees-TEE.) 'We did agree, but you yourself asked for a postponement.' «Разве я отказываюсь?» (RAZ-vee ya at-KA-zy-va-yus?) 'Am I refusing, then?' Four observations. First, ведь opens the turn and frames the agreement as a shared premise, which is a softer opening than a bare assertion and is the particle version of the disagreement technique in lesson 87. Second, -то in договаривались-то concedes the point while marking it as already settled, so the speaker can concede without losing the argument; the hyphen is obligatory. Third, же in вы же сами presses on the other party's own action, and сами doubles the pressure, so the particle and the pronoun are doing the same work from two directions. Fourth, разве turns a denial into a question, which invites the other side to withdraw the accusation instead of defending against it. Remove the four particles and the exchange becomes a sequence of flat claims that any reader would hear as a quarrel.
depth.mistake: Four errors define the learner's version of this lesson. The first is translating же as 'same' or 'also' and producing sentences about identity where the speaker meant emphasis. The second is hyphenating же, ведь and ли, or writing -то separately; the spelling rule is fixed: бы, же, ли separate, -то, -ка, -де hyphenated. The third is putting ли first, as in «Ли ты знаешь?», which is impossible because ли is unstressed and must lean on a preceding word; the correct order is «Знаешь ли ты?». The fourth is register: scattering же and ведь through a report or a formal letter, where they read as spoken asides and make the writer sound either chummy or aggrieved. There is also a transfer error specific to Spanish, where pues and ya carry similar stance functions and sit comfortably at the start of a clause; a Spanish speaker who transfers that placement produces «Ведь, я говорил» with a pause and a comma, while Russian wants the particle glued to the word it leans on, «Ведь я говорил», with no pause. Diagnostic for all five: cover the particle and ask whether the sentence still says the same proposition; if it does, the particle is stance and you should check its position and its register, not its dictionary meaning.
depth.application: Take a message you have written in Russian in the last month, or write one now of four or five sentences to a colleague about a delayed task. Rewrite it twice: once with no particles at all, and once with at least three particles chosen from же, ведь, -то, даже and именно. Read both aloud. The first version should sound neutral to the point of coldness; the second should sound like a person with a position. Then underline each particle and write beside it what assumption it points at, in English. If you cannot name the assumption, the particle is decoration and should go. Finally, convert the second version into a formal written note by removing every particle and replacing the stance with an explicit sentence, for example «Напоминаю, что вы обещали отправить файл» (na-pee-mee-NA-yoo, shto vy a-bee-SHCHAL-ee at-PRA-veet fyle), 'I remind you that you promised to send the file'. That last step is the register skill: stance expressed by grammar in speech, by explicit wording in writing.
depth.summary: Particles are the class Russian uses for stance, because case, aspect and word order are already busy with other work. The intensifying pair же and ведь point at shared ground, one as pressure and one as justification; -то isolates a topic and implies its alternative; ли opens a clause as a question and must stand second; разве and неужели colour the question as surprise and disbelief; даже escalates one element. Position is not decoration: particles lean on the word they modify, and ли's lack of stress is what forces the verb to the front. Spelling follows the class: бы, же and ли separate, -то and -ка with a hyphen. Use them in speech and messages, and replace them with explicit wording in formal writing, because a particle cannot be translated by a synonym, only by a different sentence.

lessons.title: Negation and its scope: не, ни, and the double negative that is not a mistake
lessons.explanation: Russian negation has two words and one rule, and the rule is the part English speakers get wrong. не denies: it stands before the constituent it denies, and it is the word that turns a statement into a negative one. ни does not deny on its own; it reinforces a denial that is already there. The Russian Wikipedia article on negative pronouns states the consequence exactly: the basic rule for using никто and ничто is obligatory negative concord, that is, a pronoun with the prefix ни- requires the negative particle не in the predicate. So «Никто ничего не сказал» (neek-TO nee-che-VO ne ska-ZAL), 'nobody said anything', is not a double negative that cancels itself; it is the only grammatical form. alphaDictionary calls this the Multiple Negation Rule: 'If the verb is negated in a clause, all the simple indefinite pronouns in the same phrase must also be negated.' Spanish speakers already have this rule and should trust it; English speakers have to unlearn the idea that two negatives make a positive. The paradigm has two halves, and the stress tells them apart. The simple negatives are stressed on the final syllable: никто (neek-TO), ничего (nee-che-VO), нигде (nee-GDYE), никогда (nee-kag-DA), никакой (nee-ka-KOY). The predicative negatives built with не- are stressed on the first syllable: нечего (NYE-che-va), некого (NYE-ka-va), негде (NYE-gdye), некогда (NYE-kag-da). The predicative set means 'there is no thing, no person, no place, no time' and it is used with an infinitive rather than with a conjugated verb: Мне нечего сказать (mnye NYE-che-va ska-ZAT), 'I have nothing to say'. The simple set is used with a negated verb: Я ничего не сказал (ya nee-che-VO ne ska-ZAL), 'I said nothing'. Both halves are clitics in the sense that the preposition goes inside them, not before them: ни с кем (nee s kyem), 'with nobody', не о чём (ne O chem), 'about nothing', ни у кого (nee oo ka-VO), 'at nobody's'. The other negation that is not about pronouns is the genitive after нет and after a negated verb. У меня нет времени (oo mee-NYA nyet VRYE-mee-nee), 'I have no time', is fixed: нет always takes the genitive. After a negated verb the genitive is a tendency rather than a law: it is normal with abstract nouns and with objects that are not definite, «Он не прочитал ни одной книги» (on ne pra-chee-TAL nee ad-NOY KNEE-gee), while a definite object stays accusative, «Он не прочитал книгу, которую я дал» (on ne pra-chee-TAL KNEE-goo, ka-TO-roo-yoo ya dal).
lessons.example: A short report of a meeting, then the same report with the negation removed so that you can see what each negative was doing. На собрании никто ничего не предложил. Ни один отдел не прислал цифры. Обсуждать было нечего, и спорить было не о чём. Я не могу не сказать, что сроки сорваны. (na sab-RA-nee neek-TO nee-che-VO ne preed-la-ZHEEL. nee a-DEEN at-DYEL ne prees-LAL TSEEF-ry. ab-soozh-DAT BYE-la NYE-che-va, ee SPO-reet BYE-la ne O chem. ya ne ma-GOO ne ska-ZAT, shto SRO-kee sar-VA-ny.) 'At the meeting nobody proposed anything. Not one department sent figures. There was nothing to discuss, and there was nothing to argue about. I cannot fail to say that the deadlines have been missed.' Now the affirmative version: На собрании кто-то что-то предложил. Каждый отдел прислал цифры. Обсуждать было что, и спорить было о чём. Я могу сказать, что сроки сорваны. (na sab-RA-nee KTO-ta SHTA-ta preed-la-ZHEEL. KAzh-dy at-DYEL prees-LAL TSEEF-ry. ab-soozh-DAT BYE-la shto, ee SPO-reet BYE-la a CHYOM. ya ma-GOO ska-ZAT, shto SRO-kee sar-VA-ny.) 'Someone proposed something. Every department sent figures. There was something to discuss and something to argue about. I can say that the deadlines have been missed.' Four mechanical facts are visible in the pair. First, every negative pronoun in the first version is matched by не in its clause, four clauses and four не. Second, ни один is a separate construction with a genitive singular noun after it, and it too requires не: ни один отдел не прислал. Third, the predicative forms нечего and не о чём take an infinitive and no conjugated verb, which is why the clause has no subject; they are the negation version of lesson 83's subjectless sentences. Fourth, «не могу не сказать» contains two не and means 'I must say', not 'I cannot say': the two negatives reinforce the obligation rather than cancelling it, and a translator who counts negatives as signs will get the sentence exactly backwards.
lessons.question: You want to say 'Nobody sent anything'. A learner writes «Никто ничего послал». What is wrong, and what is the rule?
lessons.answer: The verb is missing its не, so the sentence is ungrammatical; the rule is obligatory negative concord, which requires не in the predicate whenever a ни- pronoun stands in the clause: «Никто ничего не послал».
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because the two negative pronouns already carry the negation and a third negative would cancel them.
lessons.correction: The distracter is the English rule imported wholesale. In English, 'nobody sent anything' needs one negative; adding a second produces a positive, which is why English speakers treat не as optional or as an error. Russian treats it as obligatory: the ни- pronoun marks the scope and не marks the predicate, and the two are the two halves of one construction. Note also that Russian does not use the bare negative as a modifier in the English way: there is no equivalent of 'nobody sent nothing' as a positive. The sentence «Никто ничего не послал» has three negative elements and means exactly one thing.

depth.definitions: Negation is the grammatical marking of a false or absent proposition. Scope is the part of the sentence that the negation covers: in «Он не послал отчёт» the scope is the sending, in «Он послал не отчёт» it is the object. Negative concord is the requirement that several negative words agree within one clause rather than cancel each other. Simple negative pronouns (никто, ничто, никакой, нигде, никогда) carry final stress and combine with a negated verb; predicative negatives (нечего, некого, негде, некогда) carry initial stress, mean 'there is no X', and combine with an infinitive. Genitive of negation is the use of the genitive rather than the accusative for the object of a negated verb or after нет. Prerequisites: the genitive after нет from lesson 33, the genitive plural of lesson 54, the subjectless constructions of lesson 83, and the scope discussion of lesson 101, which supplies the position rule that this lesson applies to pronouns.
depth.mechanism: The system works by dividing labour between a marker of scope and a marker of polarity. ни- marks the scope: it says 'this element is the one that does not exist'. не marks the polarity of the predicate. Because both are needed, the clause ends up with several negative-looking words that all point the same way. This is why the rule is stable across registers and why partial versions sound wrong rather than merely awkward: «Никто ничего послал» has scope markers without a polarity marker, and «Никто ничего не послал» has both. The predicative set works differently because it contains its own polarity: нечего is not 'nothing' plus a separate negation, it is a single word meaning 'there is no thing', and that is why it takes an infinitive instead of a conjugated verb and why the clause has no grammatical subject. The clitic behaviour follows from the same history: ни and не are proclitics that attach to the following word, and when that word is a prepositional phrase, the clitic attaches to the preposition, not to the pronoun, producing ни с кем and не о чём rather than the impossible с никого and о ничём. The genitive of negation is the residue of an older partitive logic: absence is expressed as the absence of a quantity, and quantities take the genitive, which is why нет is followed by the genitive in every register and why abstract nouns prefer the genitive after a negated verb.
depth.secondExample: A library counter, where the two halves of the paradigm meet. «У вас нет этой книги?» (oo vas nyet EH-tay KNEE-gee?) 'Do you not have this book?' «Нет, к сожалению, ни одного экземпляра не осталось.» (nyet, k sa-zha-LYE-nee-yoo, nee ad-na-VO ek-zem-PLYA-ra ne as-TA-las.) 'No, unfortunately, not a single copy is left.' «Тогда мне нечего читать в выходные.» (tag-DA mnye NYE-che-va chee-TAT v vy-khad-NY-ye.) 'Then I have nothing to read at the weekend.' «Может быть, ни у кого из отдела нет этой книги?» (MO-zhet byt, nee oo ka-VO eez at-DYEL-la nyet EH-tay KNEE-gee?) 'Perhaps nobody in the department has this book?' Four observations. First, «нет этой книги» is the genitive after нет, and the demonstrative and the noun both take the genitive ending, so the case runs through the whole phrase. Second, «ни одного экземпляра не осталось» pairs ни один with a genitive singular and не with the verb, which is the concord rule in its most explicit form. Third, «нечего читать» is predicative and takes the infinitive, and the sentence has no nominative subject at all. Fourth, «ни у кого нет» shows the preposition inside the pronoun, and the genitive after нет again. A learner who says «с никого» or «о ничём» has understood the meaning and missed the clitic, which is the single most audible error in this lesson.
depth.mistake: Five errors account for most failures here. The first is dropping не, as in «Никто ничего сказал», which comes from English and produces an ungrammatical clause. The second is using ничего where нечего belongs: «Мне ничего сказать» instead of «Мне нечего сказать», which confuses 'I have nothing to say' with a sentence that has no verb to attach to. The third is putting the preposition outside the pronoun: «с никого», «о ничём», «к никому», where Russian wants ни с кого, ни о чём, ни к кому. The fourth is applying the genitive of negation as a law and producing «Я не прочитал книги, которую ты дал» for a definite book, where the accusative is the natural choice because the object is identified. The fifth is reading double negation with English arithmetic and concluding that «Я не могу не согласиться» means 'I cannot agree', when it means the opposite. Spanish speakers avoid the first four errors more easily than English speakers because Spanish has concord and clitic climbing of a similar kind, but they inherit the fifth from any language that treats negatives as signs, and they sometimes transfer the bare «nada» as a complete answer where Russian prefers «Ничего» with the appropriate intonation. Diagnostic: count the negatives in your clause and check that exactly one of them is не on the predicate and that every other one is a ни- word inside the same clause.
depth.application: Write six affirmative sentences about your work or study, each with a subject, a verb and an object, for example «Коллега прислал отчёт», «У меня есть время», «Кто-то позвонил». Turn each into a negative in two ways: once with the negated verb and the appropriate ни- pronoun, and once with a predicative negative and an infinitive. Then take three of them and add a prepositional phrase with a negative pronoun, checking that the preposition sits inside: ни с кем, ни о чём, ни у кого. Finally, write one sentence with «не могу не» and one with «ни один», read the whole set aloud, and mark the stress on every negative word, because the initial versus final stress distinction is the only audible difference between the two halves of the paradigm. Fifteen minutes, one page, and you will have produced every structure this lesson describes.
depth.summary: Russian negation divides the work: ни- marks what does not exist, не marks the predicate, and both are required in the same clause. The simple negatives take final stress and a negated verb; the predicative negatives take initial stress and an infinitive, and they produce subjectless clauses. Prepositions go inside the pronoun, never before it. нет always takes the genitive, and a negated verb tends towards the genitive for indefinite and abstract objects while keeping the accusative for definite ones. Two negatives in Russian reinforce, they do not cancel, which is why «не могу не сказать» means 'I must say' and why «Никто ничего не сказал» is the only correct spelling of 'nobody said anything'.

lessons.title: The unreal and the wished-for: бы, если бы, хотел бы, чтобы
lessons.explanation: Russian builds unreality with one invariable word and one tense. The word is бы, it never changes shape, and it attaches to a past-tense form. The Russian Wikipedia article on the subjunctive states the grammar plainly: verbs in this mood have no morphological marking of tense or person, time is carried by lexical means such as вчера or на следующей неделе or by the situation, person is carried by personal pronouns, and the mood is formed by combining a past-tense verb with the invariable particle бы, or by combining бы with an infinitive. This is why the counterfactual sounds like a past tense even when it refers to the present or the future: Если бы я знал (YEs-lee by ya ZNAL), 'if I knew, if I had known', is past in form and unreal in meaning, and the context decides which time you mean. The conditional sentence normally carries бы twice, once in the if-clause and once in the main clause: Если бы вы снизили цену, мы бы подписали договор (YEs-lee by vy snee-ZEE-lee TSEE-noo, my by pod-pee-SA-lee da-ga-VOR), 'if you lowered the price, we would sign the contract'. Colloquial Russian often drops the second бы, and careful writing usually keeps both. The second construction is чтобы, which is что plus бы fused into one word and used for purpose and for wishes about someone else's action. With one subject, чтобы takes the infinitive: Я пришёл, чтобы помочь (ya pree-SHYOL, SHTA-by pa-MOCH), 'I came in order to help'. With two subjects, чтобы takes a past-tense form: Я хочу, чтобы вы проверили (ya kha-CHOO, SHTA-by vy pra-VYE-ree-lee), 'I want you to check'. Those two patterns are not interchangeable, and the choice is decided by whether the person doing the second action is the same as the person doing the first. The polite conditional is the third use and the one you will need first in professional life: Я хотел бы уточнить (ya kha-TEL by oo-tach-NEET), 'I would like to clarify', and Не могли бы вы подтвердить сроки? (ne mag-LEE by vy pod-tveer-DEET SRO-kee?), 'could you confirm the dates?'. Both are softer than the indicative and both are standard in correspondence, which is the register lesson 97 described. One spelling trap belongs here. что бы, written in two words, is the interrogative pronoun plus бы, 'what would', as in Что бы ты сделал? (shto by ty SDE-lal), 'what would you do?'. чтобы, written as one word, is the conjunction and the purpose marker. The pause and the stress fall differently, and the written form is the only guide in a text.
lessons.example: A negotiation, first as it actually happens and then with the unreal forms removed so that the difference is audible. «Если бы вы снизили цену на пять процентов, мы бы подписали договор сегодня.» (YEs-lee by vy snee-ZEE-lee tsee-NOO na pyat pra-TSEN-taf, my by pod-pee-SA-lee da-ga-VOR see-VOD-nya.) 'If you lowered the price by five percent, we would sign the contract today.' «Мы бы и рады, но маржа не позволяет.» (my by ee RA-dy, no MAR-zha ne paz-va-LYA-yet.) 'We would be glad to, but the margin does not allow it.' «Не могли бы вы пересмотреть сроки?» (ne mag-LEE by vy pee-ree-smat-RYET SRO-kee?) 'Could you reconsider the dates?' «Я хотел бы, чтобы вы подтвердили объём до пятницы.» (ya kha-TEL by, SHTA-by vy pod-tveer-DEE-lee ab-YOM da PYAT-nee-tsy.) 'I would like you to confirm the volume by Friday.' Now the indicative version: Вы снижаете цену на пять процентов, и мы подписываем договор сегодня. Мы рады, но маржа не позволяет. Пересмотрите сроки. Подтвердите объём до пятницы. (vy snee-ZHA-ee-tye tsee-NOO na pyat pra-TSEN-taf, ee my pod-PEE-sy-va-yem da-ga-VOR see-VOD-nya. my RA-dy, no MAR-zha ne paz-va-LYA-yet. pee-ree-smat-REE-tye SRO-kee. pod-tveer-DEE-tye ab-YOM da PYAT-nee-tsy.) 'You lower the price by five percent and we sign today. We are glad, but the margin does not allow it. Reconsider the dates. Confirm the volume by Friday.' The indicative version is a set of demands. The unreal version is a set of proposals and requests, and nothing else has changed: same verbs, same aspect, same case endings. Four forms carry the change. Снизили and подписали are past-tense perfectives, and the past form is what бы needs. «Мы бы и рады» is an idiom worth memorising as a unit, because it uses бы with a short adjective and no verb at all. «Не могли бы вы» is the past form of мочь plus бы plus the infinitive, and it is the standard softener for a request. «Я хотел бы, чтобы вы подтвердили» shows the two-subject pattern: the хотел бы belongs to the speaker, the подтвердили belongs to вы, and the чтобы is written as one word because it is the conjunction.
lessons.question: A learner writes «Если бы я знаю, я бы звоню». What are the two errors, and why does the correct version repeat the past form?
lessons.answer: бы must combine with a past-tense form in both clauses, so the correct sentence is «Если бы я знал, я бы позвонил»; the past form is not past time but the shape that the unreal mood requires, and the context supplies the time.
lessons.distractor: The sentence is correct, because бы already marks the unreality and the present tense can stay in both clauses.
lessons.correction: бы is a particle, not a tense. It carries no person and no time of its own, so the verb has to supply both, and the only form it combines with is the past tense, whose -л ending also happens to carry gender and number. That is why the article says the mood has no morphological marking of tense or person: the past form and the pronoun do that work. Keeping the present tense is the commonest error, and it usually comes from translating 'if I know' first and then inserting бы as if it were the English 'would'. The second error is the same mistake in the main clause, and the repair is identical: позвонил, not звоню.

depth.definitions: The subjunctive (сослагательное наклонение) is the mood of the unreal: it presents an event as imagined, wished, hypothesised or contrary to fact. In Russian it is formed with the invariable particle бы plus a past-tense form, or бы plus an infinitive. The conditional (условное наклонение) is the if-then subtype, normally with бы in both clauses. чтобы is the fused conjunction что plus бы, used for purpose with an infinitive when the subjects are the same and with a past-tense form when they differ. The polite conditional is the use of хотел бы, не могли бы вы, я бы предложил to soften a request or an opinion. Counterfactual means the condition is known to be false, as in «Если бы я тогда согласился», 'if I had agreed then', which implies that I did not. Prerequisites: the past-tense formation and agreement of lesson 37, the aspect pairs of lessons 56 to 59 because the choice of perfective or imperfective survives into the unreal, the если and когда clauses of lesson 48, and the request register of lesson 97.
depth.mechanism: The construction works by borrowing a form and reassigning its meaning. The past tense is borrowed because it is the only form in Russian that carries gender and number without carrying person, and the unreal mood needs to be able to say who without saying when. Once the past form is detached from past time, бы marks the detachment, and the result is a verb that names an event without placing it on the time line. That is why the same form can refer to the present, the past or the future, and why the context has to do the placing. The double бы in conditionals follows from the logic of the construction: each clause contains its own unreal event, and each needs its own marker. The single бы of colloquial speech is a deletion, not a different rule, and it survives because the first бы has already set the unreal frame for the whole sentence. чтобы works by the same logic in a subordinate clause: the purpose or the wish is itself unreal at the moment of speaking, so the clause takes бы, and the tense of the verb depends on whether the wisher and the actor are the same person. When they are the same, the infinitive is available and the чтобы is not strictly necessary for purpose; when they differ, the past form is obligatory because the infinitive would leave the actor unidentified.
depth.secondExample: Now a personal counterfactual, where the time reference is past and the regret is explicit. «Если бы я тогда согласился, я бы сейчас работал в другом городе.» (YEs-lee by ya tag-DA sag-la-SEEL-sya, ya by see-CHAS ra-BO-tal v droo-GOM GO-ra-dye.) 'If I had agreed then, I would be working in another city now.' «Но я не согласился, и теперь жалею об этом.» (no ya ne sag-la-SEEL-sya, ee tee-PYER zha-LYE-yoo ab EH-tam.) 'But I did not agree, and now I regret it.' «Жаль, что я не согласился.» (zhal, shto ya ne sag-la-SEEL-sya.) 'It is a pity that I did not agree.' «Хоть бы кто-нибудь предложил ещё раз.» (khot by KTO-nee-bood preed-la-ZHEEL yeshchyo raz.) 'If only someone would offer again.' Four points. First, the if-clause has a past perfective, согласился, and the main clause has an imperfective past, работал, because the working would have been an ongoing state rather than a completed act; aspect survives inside the unreal, and this is the detail that separates a good sentence from a correct one. Second, the time words тогда and сейчас sit outside the verb forms and do all the temporal work, exactly as the grammar article says. Third, the indicative follow-up «я не согласился» is the sentence that establishes the counterfactuality: without it the conditional is a hypothesis, with it the hypothesis is marked false. Fourth, «Хоть бы кто-нибудь предложил» is a wish with бы and no если, and the particle хоть adds the colour of impatience; this pattern is extremely common in speech and almost absent from formal writing.
depth.mistake: Five errors dominate. The first is a present-tense verb after бы, as in «Если бы я знаю», which is ungrammatical. The second is doubling бы in the same clause, «Если бы я бы знал», which comes from over-applying the pattern; one бы per clause is enough. The third is using чтобы with an infinitive when the subjects differ, «Я хочу, чтобы я проверил», where the natural sentence is either «Я хочу проверить» or «Я хочу, чтобы вы проверили». The fourth is confusing что бы with чтобы in writing: «Что бы ты сделал?» is a question about a hypothetical action, «Я хочу, чтобы ты пришёл» is a wish about someone else's action, and the single letter decides the reading. The fifth is register: a formal letter that says «Снизьте цену» where the relationship calls for «Не могли бы вы снизить цену», which reads as a demand rather than a request. English speakers make the first two most often because 'would' is a separate word that can be sprinkled anywhere; Spanish speakers make the third, because Spanish uses the subjunctive in a single clause where Russian needs чтобы with a past form and a stated subject. Diagnostic: circle every бы and check that each one stands in a clause with a past-tense form or an infinitive, and that the actor of each clause is identifiable.
depth.application: Write six sentences about your own work. Two counterfactual conditionals in the past, for example «Если бы мы начали раньше, мы бы успели» (YEs-lee by my na-CHA-lee RAN-she, my by oos-PYE-lee), 'if we had started earlier, we would have made it'. Two polite requests with не могли бы вы plus the infinitive, addressed to a colleague you do not know well. Two wishes with хочу, чтобы plus a past form and a different subject, for example «Я хочу, чтобы вы проверили цифры» (ya kha-CHOO, SHTA-by vy pra-VYE-ree-lee TSEE-fry). Then rewrite each pair once with the second бы dropped, and decide which version you would send and which you would only say. Finally, underline every verb and label its aspect, because the aspect choice is what makes a counterfactual precise: a perfective in the if-clause presents a single completed act, an imperfective presents a state or a habit, and the difference changes what the regret is about.
depth.summary: The unreal mood in Russian is one particle and one form: бы plus a past-tense verb, with no marking of tense or person of its own, so the context and the pronouns do that work. Conditionals carry бы in both clauses, and the colloquial single бы is a deletion of the second. чтобы is что plus бы fused, and it takes an infinitive when the subjects match and a past form when they differ. хотел бы and не могли бы вы are the polite conditional, the standard softener of professional requests. Aspect survives into the unreal and is what makes a hypothesis precise. Keep one бы per clause, keep the past form after it, and keep что бы and чтобы apart in writing.

lessons.title: свой: the possessive that points back at the subject
lessons.explanation: свой is the possessive pronoun Russian uses when the owner is the subject of the clause. It means 'my own, your own, his own, her own, our own, their own' depending on who the subject is, and it agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. That single sentence covers most of the lesson. Compare «Он любит свою работу» (on LYO-beet sva-YOO ra-BO-too), 'he loves his work', with «Он любит его работу» (on LYO-beet ee-VO ra-BO-too), 'he loves his work' in the sense of someone else's. In the first, свою agrees with работу, which is feminine accusative, and points back to он. In the second, его is indeclinable and points outside the clause, so the sentence now says that he loves another man's work. alphaDictionary states the rule in the same terms: the possessive reflexive 'is used to refer to a possessor identical with the subject of a sentence'. The declension is the soft adjective pattern you already know from чей. Masculine свой, своего, своему, свой or своего, своим, о своём. Feminine своя, своей, свою, своей, свою, своей. Neuter своё, своего, своему, своё, своим, о своём. Plural свои, своих, своим, свои, своими, о своих. The stress moves in the plural and in the oblique masculine and neuter forms: своё (sva-YO), свои (sva-EE), своего (sva-ee-VO), своим (sva-EEM), своих (sva-EEkh). The third-person possessives его, её and их do not decline at all, which the Russian Wikipedia article on possessive pronouns notes as the exception to the rule that this class declines like adjectives: 'Изменяются как прилагательные, за исключением притяжательных местоимений третьего лица.' That is why его работа, его работу and о его работе all keep the same его, and why the form cannot tell you whose work it is. Three practical consequences follow. First, свой cannot be the subject or stand alone as a noun phrase in the nominative: it is attributive, so it needs a noun to agree with. Second, in the first and second person, свой competes with мой and твой, and the choice is a matter of emphasis rather than correctness: «Я взял свою книгу» and «Я взял мою книгу» are both possible, and the first is the more usual because it keeps the reference inside the clause. Third, in a subordinate clause свой points to the subject of that clause, not to the subject of the whole sentence, so «Он сказал, что Мария любит свою работу» means that Maria loves Maria's work, while «Он сказал, что любит свою работу» means that he loves his own.
lessons.example: Four sentences, each with a different reference. 1. Мария показала свою фотографию. (ma-REE-ya pa-ka-ZA-la sva-YOO fa-ta-GRA-fee-yoo.) 'Maria showed a photograph of herself, or her own photograph.' The reference is unambiguous: свою points at Мария, who is the subject. 2. Мария показала её фотографию. (ma-REE-ya pa-ka-ZA-la ee-YO fa-ta-GRA-fee-yoo.) 'Maria showed her photograph.' Now the reference is ambiguous between another woman's photograph and a photograph of Maria, because её carries no link to the subject. 3. Иван принёс свои документы, а коллега принёс свои. (ee-VAN pree-NYOS sva-EE da-koo-MYEN-ty, a ka-LYE-ga pree-NYOS sva-EE.) 'Ivan brought his documents, and the colleague brought his own.' Each свои points to its own clause's subject, so the two sets are different sets, and the sentence needs no further clarification. 4. Иван принёс свои документы, а коллега принёс его документы. (ee-VO da-koo-MYEN-ty.) 'Ivan brought his documents, and the colleague brought Ivan's.' The switch from свои to его is the whole difference between two sets and one set. Now the cases, because agreement is where the endings matter: Я взял свою книгу. (ya vzyal sva-YOO KNEE-goo.) 'I took my book.' Accusative feminine, agreeing with книгу. Он доволен своей работой. (on da-VO-leen sva-YEY ra-BO-tay.) 'He is satisfied with his work.' Instrumental feminine, agreeing with работой. Мы говорили о своих планах. (my ga-va-REE-lee a sva-EEkh PLA-nakh.) 'We talked about our plans.' Prepositional plural, agreeing with планах. Она вернулась в свой город. (a-NA veer-NOO-las f svoy GO-rat.) 'She returned to her own city.' Accusative masculine inanimate, which looks nominative. And one idiom that fixes the word in memory: Он сделал это своими руками. (on SDE-lal EH-ta sva-EE-mee roo-KA-mee.) 'He did it with his own hands.'
lessons.question: A colleague says «Он попросил секретаря отправить свою презентацию». Who does the presentation belong to, and why is the sentence worth avoiding in writing?
lessons.answer: свой points to the subject of the clause, so the presentation is his own, but with an infinitive complement the reference can also be read as the secretary's, which makes the sentence ambiguous; the unambiguous repairs are «отправить его презентацию» or a restructured clause naming the owner.
lessons.distractor: свой always refers to the nearest noun, so the presentation belongs to the secretary, and the sentence is unambiguous.
lessons.correction: свой refers to the subject, not to the nearest noun. The subject of the sentence is он, so the default reading is that he asked the secretary to send his own presentation. But infinitive complements are exactly where the rule becomes unstable, because the secretary is the understood agent of отправить, and readers can assign свой to that agent. This is a known grey area, not a beginner's error, and the professional response is to avoid the construction: write «отправить его презентацию» if it is his, or «попросил, чтобы секретарь отправил свою презентацию» if it is hers. The distracter is a plausible rule of thumb that happens to be wrong, and it is the sort of half-rule that produces confident misreadings.

depth.definitions: A possessive pronoun marks the owner of a noun. Russian has three types: first and second person forms (мой, твой, наш, ваш), third person forms (его, её, их), and the reflexive possessive свой. The reflexive possessive refers to the subject of the clause in which it stands, which is why it has no nominative form of its own as a noun phrase and no person of its own. Agreement is with the possessed noun in gender, number and case, not with the owner. Anaphora is the technical name for this kind of reference back, and свой is an anaphor: it needs an antecedent, and the antecedent is the subject. Prerequisites: the adjective declension of lesson 41, the accusative of lesson 51, the dative and instrumental of lessons 61 and 63, and the clause structure of lesson 73, because свой inside a который clause points to the subject of that clause.
depth.mechanism: The pronoun exists because Russian distinguishes two kinds of possession that English leaves to context. In English, 'he loves his work' is ambiguous between his own work and another man's, and the ambiguity is usually resolved by context or by adding 'own'. Russian resolves it grammatically: свой means the subject's, его means someone else's. That is why the pair is not a stylistic choice but a referential one, and why a text that uses его where свой is meant can be read as saying something quite different about whose documents were brought. The mechanism is agreement plus antecedent. The ending of свой tracks the noun it modifies, so свою is feminine accusative because работу is feminine accusative; the reference tracks the subject, so свою points at он, она, мы or они depending on who is doing the action. Because the two tracks are independent, the same form can serve any owner: свою книгу can be 'my own book', 'your own book' or 'her own book', and only the subject tells you which. This is also why свой cannot stand as the subject itself: it has no independent reference, only a borrowed one, and a pronoun that borrows its reference cannot be the thing that supplies it.
depth.secondExample: A workplace paragraph where the distributive use does the work. «Каждый сотрудник отвечает за своё направление. Начальник отдела проверяет свои цифры, а я проверяю свои.» (KAzh-dy sat-ROOD-neek at-vee-CHA-yet za sva-YO nap-rav-LYE-nee-ye. na-CHAL-neek at-DYEL-la pra-vee-RYA-yet sva-EE TSEEF-ry, a ya pra-vee-RYA-yoo sva-EE.) 'Every employee is responsible for their own area. The head of department checks his own figures, and I check mine.' Three points. First, «каждый сотрудник ... своё направление» is distributive: each employee has a different area, and свой is what makes the sentence say so without adding «у каждого». Second, the contrast «свои ... а я ... свои» works because each свои is bound by its own subject, so the two sets are automatically different; replacing the second with его would collapse the contrast and make the sentence say that the speaker checks the head's figures. Third, the neuter form своё in the first sentence is the agreement with направление, and the plural свои in the other two is the agreement with цифры, which shows the same pronoun tracking three different nouns in three sentences. This paragraph is the model for any text about roles and responsibilities, which is why it belongs in a professional course rather than a family one.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first is using его or её where the owner is the subject: «Он любит его работу» for 'he loves his work', which says something else. The second is making свой agree with the owner rather than with the thing owned, producing «Он любит свой работа» or «Она взяла свой книгу». The third is using свой as a standalone subject or as a nominalised 'his own', as in «Свой пришёл поздно», which Russian does not allow without a noun. The fourth is overcorrection: replacing every его with свой on the assumption that свой is more Russian, which produces sentences about the subject's possessions where the text meant someone else's. English speakers make the first error constantly because English has one word for both readings, and Spanish speakers make it too, since Spanish su is equally indifferent; both languages solve the problem with 'own' or with a clarifying phrase, and Russian solves it with the pronoun. Diagnostic: for every possessive, ask who the subject of that clause is and who owns the noun; if the answers match, свой is available, and if the sentence would be ambiguous without it, свой is required.
depth.application: Take a paragraph of your own writing in Russian, at least six sentences, and underline every possessive. For each one write the subject of its clause and the owner of the noun. Where the two match, replace the possessive with свой in the correct gender, number and case; where they differ, keep его, её or их and add a clarifying noun if the reference is still unclear. Then write four sentences of your own using свою, своего, своей and своих, one per form, and check each ending against its noun rather than against the owner. Finally, take the ambiguous sentence from the question and write two unambiguous versions, one for each possible owner, which is the exercise that turns the rule into a habit.
depth.summary: свой is the possessive of the subject: it points back to whoever is doing the action in that clause, and it agrees with the thing owned in gender, number and case. его, её and их are the third-person possessives that do not decline and do not point back, which is why they can be ambiguous and why a careful writer replaces them with свой when the owner is the subject. The declension follows the soft adjective pattern, with stress moving to the ending in свои, своего, своим and своих. The pronoun cannot stand as a subject, and in subordinate clauses it follows the subject of its own clause. The professional habit is simple: before every possessive, name the subject and name the owner, and let the answer choose the word.

visual.title: Owner and noun: a two-track agreement check
visual.description: A labeled text diagram in three columns: the clause, the subject who owns, and the noun that is owned with its gender, number and case. A fourth column shows the resulting form of свой. Rendered as text steps, not as an image.
steps: Step 1, write the clause and box the subject. Take «Он доволен своей работой» and put a box around он. Label the box 'antecedent'. Every later decision depends on this box.

Step 2, find the owned noun and label its three properties. Underline работой and write 'feminine, singular, instrumental'. This is the track that decides the ending, and it has nothing to do with the person in the box.

Step 3, cross the tracks. Draw a line from the box to the possessive and write 'owner = subject, so свой'. Then read the properties from step 2 and write the form: своей. Mark that the line crosses from masculine он to feminine работой without changing anything, which is the point of the diagram.

Step 4, run the contrast row. Repeat steps 1 to 3 with «Он доволен его работой», and write in the fourth column 'его, indeclinable, owner outside the clause'. Put a warning mark beside it: the form does not change with the noun's case, so it cannot signal agreement.
